fatal_errors: The cited Sn study concerns FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx, not single-phase fcc FeCoNi, and every reported composition is already multiphase FCC/BCC.
The evidence supports increased saturation magnetization and Curie temperature, not increased coercivity; it characterizes the alloys as soft magnets and reports decreasing remanence.
The proposed FCC-to-BCC transformation at 600–700 K does not reconstruct the target intervention or its fcc/C14 dual-phase mediator.
No quantitative coercivity prediction is given, so the hypothesis does not establish that the proposed treatment would exceed 100 Oe.
The experiment cannot distinguish an intrinsic Sn effect from effects of BCC fraction, Cu-rich precipitates, unknown phases, thermal history, or the added Cu and Al.
explanation: The response recognizes the low-coercivity baseline and proposes a testable compositional intervention, but it does not recover the target FeCoNiTi dual-phase fcc/C14 strategy, its rapid-quench processing, antiferromagnetic sublattice coupling, spin canting/domain-wall pinning mechanism, transition assignments, or the approximately 667 Oe coercivity at 400 K. More importantly, its own evidence does not validate the central coercivity claim: the cited work reports changes in phase fraction, Curie temperature, magnetization, and remanence in a chemically different, initially multiphase soft-magnetic alloy. The dose-series experiment has a nominal falsification rule, but lacks matched Cu/Al-free controls, fixed thermal histories, quantitative phase-fraction and microstructural controls, and a threshold such as Hc greater than 100 Oe. Thus it is neither an evidence-supported alternative nor a reconstruction of the hidden result.
